interactions.summary: Jiang continues the Ulysses discussion by arguing that individuality is socially anchored, then answers why Ulysses is worse than thieves or murderers: he betrays roots, family roles, and even the conditions that make identity possible, which is why exile is felt as identity death.
interactions.speaker_attribution: Jiang answer to student question with student follow-up

interactions.summary: A student returns to the serpent image and links it to the original serpent robbing Adam and Eve of paradise, and Jiang strengthens the link by noting Milton's devils also end as snakes.

claims.claim: Jiang insists that individuality is only real when anchored to other people rather than imagined as a solitary possession.
Jiang answers that Ulysses is worse than theft because he harms not strangers but his own family and roots, abandoning the people to whom he owes role and care.
Jiang uses Dante's own exile from Florence to argue that exile can be worse than execution because it strips away the social world that makes a person who he is.
The student's serpent allusion Jiang endorses is that the thieves' transformation repeats the original serpent's robbery of Adam and Eve's paradise.
Jiang notes a symmetry with Milton: in Paradise Lost the devils end as snakes, reinforcing the serpent as an image of corrupted desire and theft.

signature_moments.moment: Exile is worse than execution because it does not merely end life; it takes away the social body that makes identity possible.
signature_moments.why_it_matters: It ties Ulysses, Dante's biography, and Jiang's social theory of the self into one reusable claim.

signature_moments.moment: The serpent is not just a punishment prop; it is the old robber of paradise returning as the thieves' proper shape.
signature_moments.why_it_matters: It deepens the Genesis line from earlier packets into a broader literary-theological symmetry.

glossary_terms.definition_or_usage: Jiang's claim that exile destroys the social setting that lets a person be who he is, making it worse than mere bodily death in some contexts.
The familial and communal ties Ulysses betrays; losing them leaves ambition rootless.
